sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The page is clear in a few seconds.** The headline says what the ferry does and how long the crossing takes ("Cross the bay in twelve calm minutes"). The paragraph adds how often boats leave and what you can bring. There is only one button, and "See the timetable" names exactly what it opens. A first-time viewer can tell what the page is for and what to do next.
- **Nothing on the page is extra.** It has a small blue brand line, the headline, the paragraph, three benefit lines and one blue button, with no boxes, rules or decoration. Only the brand name and the button are blue, and the type is one family throughout. The calm white space and centred, level layout match the "calm" promise in the headline and don't fight it.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** What matters first (hierarchy): applies.

**Findings**
1. **Below the first element, can you tell each level of the text (title, headings, body, captions) from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same?** No. The paragraph (about x 290–990, y 250–335) looks to be about 20 px. The three feature lines below it, "Bicycles travel free / Seats on the open deck / Hot drinks on board" (about x 540–740, y 368–455), look to be about 18 px. Both use the same regular weight, the same near-black and the same centring, and the list has no bullet, icon or other marker. So the viewer sees two sizes a pixel or two apart that don't read as two levels. The list looks like a slightly smaller extra paragraph or a mistake, not a set of quick selling points, and the three benefits get skimmed past on the way to the button. This matches Bringhurst's warning against sizes picked one at a time (*The Elements of Typographic Style*, 3.1.1 "Don't compose without a scale"). It also matches Dair's point that a difference meant to show must be obvious, not one step (*Design with Type*, ch. 8). Fix: make the list a level you can see at a glance. Use the same size as the body and separate it by structure (markers or icons, a left-aligned block, a row of three), or by weight or colour. Don't leave it a near-miss size. Convention, minor: the page still works, but the benefits are weaker than they should be. Measure both sizes to confirm the gap.

**What's working.**
- The headline wins by a wide margin. At roughly 2.5× the body size and in heavy bold, it is the only possible starting point. It also carries the offer ("twelve calm minutes"), so the focal point and the message are the same thing.
- The small blue bold "Coastal Ferry Co." eyebrow and the blue button use the same colour, and that colour is the only one on the page. The brand line sits quietly above the headline, and the button stands out as the one action after the text. The order from headline to action is clear without any extra weight.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (each level of text distinguishable, no near-same sizes)

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies. This is a single centred column on what looks like a 1280×800 frame. I worked from the whole image, because the crop script could not be run here (Bash was refused).

**Findings**
1. **Is the space inside each group clearly smaller than the space between groups, so each heading sits nearer the text it introduces?** No. The three feature lines at y≈368–455 are spaced about 33 px apart. That is almost the same as the paragraph's line spacing of about 31 px (y≈250–335). The gap between the paragraph and the list is only about 35 px, much like the gaps headline→paragraph (about 40 px) and list→button (about 40 px). The list is also the same size, weight and colour as the paragraph, centred, with no bullets. Because space is the only thing that could set it apart, it reads as three short extra lines of the paragraph rather than a separate set of benefits, and the "free bicycles" point loses its punch. Source: Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. II, on grouping by proximity. Fix: make the gap above and below the list clearly bigger than its own line spacing (about twice as much), and tighten the list's spacing, so it stands as its own group. Defect. Weight: minor.
2. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** No. The whole stack runs from y≈70 to y≈548. That leaves about 70 px above it and about 250 px of empty white below. The weight sits in the top two-thirds and the bottom looks unfinished, as if an image or a next section failed to load. Source: Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance". Fix: if this frame is the whole first screen, move the stack down to sit just above the optical centre, or put something in the lower band (a photo of the boat or bay would also help the copy). If more content follows straight below in the live page, this is fine. Defect. Weight: minor.
3. **Is each centered or symmetric placement of blocks or of the main subject there for a reason the piece shows, rather than by habit?** No. Every block sits on the x=640 axis: eyebrow, the two-line headline, the three-line paragraph, the list and the button. Centring the short headline and the button suits a one-message hero. Centring the three-line paragraph and the list gives them ragged left edges, so each line starts somewhere new and the list is harder to scan. Source: Tschichold, *The New Typography*, "The principles of the new typography". Approved fix: keep centring for a few short lines, and set the longer text and the list on a shared left edge (or arrange the blocks asymmetrically in content order). Convention. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- Every element sits exactly on one centre axis. There are no near-misses of a few pixels, so the column reads as deliberate.
- The empty space is gathered into wide side margins and one open band. The space isn't scattered between elements, so the eye has room around the headline.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the page continues just below y=800. That decides whether finding 2 is a real empty bottom or just a crop.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 10 yes, 3 no (space inside groups smaller than between groups; visual weight balances; centring there for a reason), 0 unsure

I'm done with the walk and the deep read, and am writing the report now. Two of the three doubtful lines came out fine: the source draws the line for centred paragraphs at four or more lines, and the list items are single lines with no bullets.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do headings and captions break at phrase boundaries, never between a number and its unit or inside a name?** No. The headline (about x 345–935, y 110–220) breaks as "Cross the bay in twelve / calm minutes". The number ends line 1 and its unit, "minutes", starts line 2, with "calm" in between. The headline's one real promise is "twelve minutes", and a reader takes it in two pieces: "twelve" hangs on the first line and the claim only comes together after the line break. Bringhurst (*The Elements of Typographic Style*, 2.4.6) says to keep short numerical expressions together. The entry notes that no source states the heading-break rule as such, so treat the heading part as common sense. Fix: break as "Cross the bay in / twelve calm minutes" so the whole promise sits on one line, using a non-breaking space or a set break. **Convention.** Weight: **minor**. The headline still reads correctly, but the key claim would land more cleanly.

**What's working.**
- The type is all one family in a clear scale: a ~56 px bold headline with tight two-line leading, ~20 px body, ~18 px list items, and a ~14 px bold blue eyebrow. Each size has an obvious job, and weight and colour do the finer work instead of extra sizes.
- The body paragraph is comfortable to read. Its lines run about 74 characters, at the top of the 45–75 range, with generous leading and dark grey on white. Because it is only three lines, centring it doesn't hurt reading.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (headings break at phrase boundaries, not between a number and its unit)

First read: the eye lands on the large near-black headline, drops through the grey-black body text, and stops on the blue "See the timetable" button. It's a calm, sparse ferry landing page. Job (assumed): a hero section that gets visitors to open the timetable.

Walk (Color):
- Small palette: yes. White, near-black text and one blue, used on the eyebrow and the button.
- Strong colour kept to a small area: yes. Blue covers only the button (about 210×55 px) and the eyebrow.
- Clear range of light and dark: yes. Dark text on white, and the button is a dark block that holds up in grayscale.
- Warm forward, cool recedes: yes. The piece has no warm colour. The blue button comes forward through saturation and value, which serves it.
- Matching colours look the same: yes. The eyebrow blue and the button blue read as one hue.
- No vibrating edges: yes. White on mid-dark blue doesn't vibrate.
- Status colours used for their usual meaning: yes. Blue is the brand and action colour, which is its usual web meaning.
- Colour never carries meaning alone: yes. The button has a filled shape and a label, and the eyebrow is text.
- Dark theme: yes (not applicable, light theme).

Every line is yes, so step 5 has no entries to open.

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **One blue does all the colour work.** It marks the brand (the "Coastal Ferry Co." eyebrow at about y=80) and the one action (the "See the timetable" button at about x=535–745, y=493–548). The only saturated area on an otherwise white and near-black page is the thing to click, so the eye ends on the action without competition.
- **Light and dark carry the structure.** The near-black headline and the dark blue button are the two darkest masses, with grey-black body text between them. The order of headline → copy → action survives in grayscale, so the hierarchy doesn't depend on hue.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Pictures: skipped. The image has no photos, illustrations, icons, logos or marks. "Coastal Ferry Co." at the top (about x 577–703, y 72–88) is set as plain blue text, not as a logo mark. Whether that text is right belongs to the Text and Color sections.

**Findings**
None.

**Checklist.** Pictures: skipped

sections.report:
**Section.** Interface: applies. There is one control, the "See the timetable" button, and the page around it is a site entry point with no navigation. I could not run the helper scripts (Bash was denied), so I judged the 1280×800 image whole and by eye, without opening the catalog entries.

**Findings**
1. **Do the navigation and components follow the conventions users know from the platform and similar products? / Do the grouping, names, and navigation show how the product's parts relate?**
   - **Where:** the whole page. There is no site header, no logo, no navigation and no footer. The only brand mark is the small blue "Coastal Ferry Co." line (about 576–704, 72–88).
   - **What the viewer meets:** a ferry company's site usually has a header with links such as Timetable, Fares, Tickets and Getting here. A visitor who wants prices, tickets or directions to the "north landing" has nowhere to go except the timetable button. They can't tell what else the site holds or how to get back to it.
   - **Why:** Jakob's law (Nielsen Norman Group). Users expect a site to work like others they know.
   - **Fix:** add a standard header with the logo and the three or four tasks a passenger comes for, and keep the hero as it is. If this capture is one section cut from a longer page that already has a header above it, this finding doesn't apply.
   - **Mark:** convention. **Weight:** major if this is the whole page, none if it is a cut-out section.
2. **Does the screen put what the user likely needs next in front of them (a prefilled default, the next action, or the information they came for) instead of making them hunt for it?**
   - **Where:** the body copy (about 290–990, 250–335) and the button (535–745, 493–548).
   - **What the viewer meets:** someone planning a crossing wants three things: when the next boat leaves, what it costs, and where to board. The page gives only "every forty minutes from early morning until late evening", which has no first or last sailing time. It gives no fare (only that bicycles travel free) and doesn't say where the north landing is. All of this sits behind a click, and the lower 250 px of the screen is empty.
   - **Fix:** show the next two or three departures, or at least the first and last sailing, plus the adult fare, right beside or above the button. Keep the button for the full timetable.
   - **Mark:** taste. The source for this line is off-list (Tognazzini). **Weight:** minor, because the button is clear and the timetable is one click away.
3. **Does every control look like what it does, buttons pressable, fields typeable, and links marked by more than color?**
   - **Where:** "Coastal Ferry Co." (about 576–704, 72–88). It is set bold in the same blue as the primary button and is the only other blue on the page.
   - **What the viewer meets:** it reads as a link, perhaps to the home page, but it doesn't look like a logo either. Users may click it and get nothing, or never realise it is the brand.
   - **Why:** this is common sense, not a catalogued rule. The page reserves the action color for the button, so blue text suggests "clickable".
   - **Fix:** if it links home, make it a real logo or lockup in a header. If it doesn't, set it in a non-link color such as the dark text color, or a muted tone.
   - **Mark:** taste. **Weight:** minor.

**What's working.**
- There is exactly one action, and nothing competes with it. The solid blue button is the only filled shape on the page, and it sits directly under the content it follows. Nobody has to hunt for it.
- The button label "See the timetable" says exactly what happens on click, in the passenger's own words. That is far better than "Learn more" or "Get started". The button is about 210×55 px, well above the 24 px minimum target size, and the white-on-blue text and the button's edge against white have strong contrast.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Focus indicator: whether the button shows a visible ring at least 2 px thick with 3:1 contrast. Keyboard users need it to find the page's only action.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 28 yes, 4 no (conventions users know; grouping and navigation show how parts relate; puts what the user needs next in front of them; every control looks like what it does), 1 unsure (focus indicator)
